newsitem.title: UK: British, U.S., French firms best meet U.S. holder demands.
newsitem.headline: British, U.S., French firms best meet U.S. holder demands.

text.p: While British and American firms most meet the demands of U.S. shareholders concerning corporate governance, a survey of the world's top five stock markets shows that French firms meet demands better than those in either Germany or Japan.

Using indicators based on guidelines promoted by British and U.S. institutional investors, corporate governance consultants Davis Global Advisors said Thursday that on a 10-scale index, Britain topped the list with a score of 7.6 and the U.S. was second with 7.2.
Among non-English speaking markets, France scored 5.3 compared with Germany's 4.4 and Japan's 3.3.

"Britain outpaced the U.S. thanks to practices that give shareholders more say over strategic corporate decisions, more boards splitting the jobs of chairman and chief executive and the adoption of national corporate governance standards," the consultants said.
Although France scored lower than the United States overall, France gave more voice to shareholders than the United States, the report noted.

French boards have to get shareholder approval before making major decisions, which could affect stock prices, while U.S. corporations do not have to consult, which often sparks shareholder rebellions.

"France also has a higher percentage of large corporations using international or American accounting standards than Germany or Japan, making it easier for international investors to evaluate French financial statements," the report said.

However, French boards "tend to be dominated by powerful chairman/chief executives, leading institutions to question the ability of directors to effectively oversee management. Moreover, companies often feature double-voting shares which dilute the ballot influence of many shareholders."
Like Germany and Japan, France lags well behind the United States and Britain in disclosure of executive pay, and proxy voting is tougher, Davis Global Advisors said.
